title: Alveolar Echinococcosis in Children
case_text:
A 5-year-old girl (height 120 cm, weight 21 kg) presented with abdominal pain, fever (38 C), and vomiting to emergency room where abdominal US demonstrated two cysts of 2.3 and 1.8 cm size with transparent fluid in the S7/8 and 1 cyst of 1 cm in S4. In addition, multiple mesenteric lymph nodes from 0.6 to 1.4 cm were detected. During further investigation positive IgG against echinococcus were found. Evaluation after 3 months showed borderline E. multilocularis IgG (ELISA) 0.881 OD (cut-off 0.82), total IgE over 1000 IU/ml (normal value < 60 IU/ml), and normal levels of hepatic enzymes. On abdominal US both cysts in S7/8 had increased to 2.6 cm and 2.1 cm, respectively, in the left lobe 0.8 cm cyst was seen with fibrinous septum (Figure 2). Despite the fact that cysts were similar to CE, definitive diagnosis could not be made because of positive serological tests for AE. Treatment with ABZ 10 mg/kg/day divided into two doses in tablets was started.
After 10 days of treatment with ABZ the girl started to complain of feet and palms' itching followed by erythema and urticarial rash. On CBC increased amount of eosinophils was found (1.71 x 109/l). The patient was given antihistamines and the symptoms were resolved. It was not clear if ABZ caused the allergic reaction; thus the drug was continued and similar symptoms did not repeat.
Despite the treatment, after 3 months the disease was still active: multiple septa, capsules, and hyperechogenic insertions appeared in all cysts. 2 months later they had even slightly enlarged (up to 2.7 cm). As there was no improvement, MRI to further specify the changes in the liver was performed (Figure 3) and revealed more lesions compared to US: multiple cysts up to 2.7 cm size in S8/5, S7/6, S7, and S2/4 were present. Lesions on MRI posed higher suspicion of CE and the diagnosis was confirmed by repeated serological tests (E. granulosus IgG 0.674 OD (cut-off 0.21)). Hepatic enzymes remained normal. Currently conservative treatment is continued.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Echinococcosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: cystic echinococcosis of the liver
